title: Digital data
everyday: How numbers, letters and pictures are stored as 0s and 1s.

screens.title: Bits, nibbles and bytes: the switches inside a computer
screens.goal: I can say why computers use 0 and 1 and count the bits in a byte.

picture.title: A wall plate of light switches
lines: Look at the wall plate in the photo. It has four light switches. Each one is pressed one way or the other, never in between. The switch on the right is pressed the other way from the three beside it. Ignore the small pictures on the switches.

A switch like this is either off or on. One switch, off or on, is called a [[bit|1]]. Off is written 0 and on is written 1. The four switches on this plate make a [[nibble|1]], 4 bits. Put two plates side by side and the eight switches make a [[byte|1]], 8 bits.
A computer chip holds billions of switches like these, only far smaller. Every photo, song and message is stored as switches that are on or off.
match: One light switch, on or off
The four switches on one plate
Two plates side by side, eight switches
picture.breaks: Real switches are big and slow. The switches in a chip are smaller than a germ. They flip billions of times a second.

img.alt: A white wall plate with four rocker light switches. The right-hand switch is rocked the opposite way to the other three.
img.cap: Four switches on one plate. Each is either one way or the other. Four switches make a nibble.

say: A computer chip is packed with billions of tiny switches like these. Each switch is either off or on.

A switch only has to tell two states apart: off or on. That is hard to get wrong. Picture a dimmer switch with ten levels instead. Level 6 and level 7 look almost the same, so they are easy to mix up. That is why computers count with only two digits, 0 and 1.
Off is written as 0. On is written as 1. One switch, one 0 or 1, is a bit.
Bit is short for binary digit. Binary means counting with only two digits, 0 and 1. So a binary digit is always 0 or 1.
A bit is the smallest thing a computer can store. Nothing is smaller than off or on.
Four bits together are a nibble. Eight bits together are a byte. So a nibble is half a byte.

A byte can hold one character. A character is one letter, digit or symbol, like k, 7 or ?. An agreed list gives each character its own byte. The letter k is given 01101011. You do not need to remember it. Every file is a long row of bytes.

play.title: Flip the eight switches
play.lead: Tap any switch to flip it on or off. The brackets under the switches show each nibble of four and the whole byte of eight. Ignore the numbers above the switches for now. The next skill uses them to read a byte as a number. The button under the switches reads All on or All off, and flips every switch.

exam.say: A bit is a binary digit. It can only take on the values 0 or 1. It is the smallest unit of storage in a computer system. A nibble is 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits.

try.stem: Pick TRUE or FALSE for each statement.

rows: Half a byte is called a nibble.

try.why: A nibble is four bits, half a byte. A bit is only ever 0 or 1.

screens.title: Binary to denary: add the headings that have a 1
screens.goal: I can change a byte from binary into denary and show my working.

anim.title: Change a byte into an everyday number, step by step
anim.lead: The numbers you count with every day, like 181, are called [[denary|1]] numbers. Press Next to watch the byte 10110101 change into a denary number. This is the working the examiner wants to see.
steps: Write a row of eight numbers called headings. Start with 1 on the far right. Moving left, each heading doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. So 128 is on the far left.
Copy the byte under the headings, one bit under each heading. Here the bits are 10110101.
Look at each 1. A 1 means count the heading above it. Those headings light up: 128, 32, 16, 4 and 1. A 0 means do not count that heading, so skip it.
Write those headings as one sum: 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1.
Add them up. 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 1 = 181. So the byte 10110101 is 181 in denary.

say: The numbers you count with every day are denary numbers. Denary uses ten digits, 0 to 9.
A computer counts with only two digits, 0 and 1. That is [[binary|1]].
To read a byte, write a number above each of its eight bits. These numbers are called headings.
The headings, from left to right, are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.
Each heading from 2 up to 128 is double the one on its right.
A 1 under a heading means count that heading. A 0 under a heading means do not count it.
To change binary into denary, add up the headings that have a 1 under them. The total is the denary number.

picture.title: Weights for a kitchen scale
lines: The photo shows real kitchen weights: 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10 and 5 g. Now picture a special set of eight weights instead. In grams, they are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Line them up in that order, heaviest on the left, just like the headings.
Each weight from 2 g up to 128 g is double the one on its right. A 1 means put that weight on a kitchen scale. A 0 means leave it off.
Take the byte from the animation, 10110101. It puts 128, 32, 16, 4 and 1 g on the scale. The scale reads 181 g. That reading is the denary number, 181.

Put all eight weights on: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255 g. With these eight weights, 255 g is the most you can make. In the same way, 11111111 is 255, the biggest number one byte can hold. A byte has only eight headings, so nothing bigger fits.
match: Putting a weight on the scale
11111111, which is 255: the most one byte can hold
picture.breaks: The real weights in the photo are 500, 200, 100, 50, 20, 10 and 5 g. They do not always double: 500 is not double 200, and 50 is not double 20. In binary, each heading left of 1 is exactly double the one on its right.

img.alt: Kitchen weights stamped in grams. The 500, 200 and 100 g weights are black iron. The 50, 20, 10 and 5 g weights are brass.
img.cap: Real kitchen weights, stamped in grams. The 500, 200 and 100 g weights are iron. The 50, 20, 10 and 5 g weights are brass.

play.title: Your turn: binary to denary
play.lead: A random byte appears. First tap each heading that has a 1 under it. Then add up the headings you tapped. Each step tells you what to do.

exam.say: Write the headings 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 above the bits. The exam calls the headings place values. Add the headings that have a 1 under them. Show the working, because the working earns a mark.
exam.src: 2021 Q6(b) mark scheme: conversion work, addition of results, 251

try.stem: What is the byte 01011010 in denary?
try.why: The bits that are 1 sit under the headings 64, 16, 8 and 2. Then 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 90.

screens.title: Denary to binary: the take-away game
screens.goal: I can turn any denary number up to 255 into eight bits and show my working.

anim.title: Change the denary number 147 into binary, step by step
anim.lead: To change denary into binary, play a game of take-away. Your number starts as the amount left. Press Next to ask one question at each heading. Can the heading be taken from the amount left?
steps: Write the eight headings, 128 on the far left down to 1 on the far right. The amount left starts as 147, the number to change.
Can 128 be taken from 147? Yes: 128 is smaller than 147. Write 1. 147 − 128 = 19, so the amount left is 19.
Can 64 be taken from 19? No: 64 is bigger than 19. Write 0. The amount left is still 19.
Can 32 be taken from 19? No: 32 is bigger than 19. Write 0. The amount left is still 19.
Can 16 be taken from 19? Yes: 16 is smaller than 19. Write 1. 19 − 16 = 3, so the amount left is 3.
Can 8 be taken from 3? No: 8 is bigger than 3. Write 0. The amount left is still 3.
Can 4 be taken from 3? No: 4 is bigger than 3. Write 0. The amount left is still 3.
Can 2 be taken from 3? Yes: 2 is smaller than 3. Write 1. 3 − 2 = 1, so the amount left is 1.
Can 1 be taken from 1? Yes: 1 is the same as 1. Write 1. 1 − 1 = 0, so the amount left is 0. So 147 is 10010011. Check: 128 + 16 + 2 + 1 = 147.

say: That was the take-away game. Write the eight headings, 128 on the far left down to 1 on the far right. Your denary number is the amount left. Start at the 128 heading.
Ask one question at every heading: can this heading be taken from the amount left?

The answer is yes if the heading is the same as the amount left, or smaller. Write a 1 under it and take it away. Use the new amount left at the next heading. For example, 64 can be taken from 86, so write 1. Then 86 − 64 = 22 is the new amount left. The answer is no if the heading is bigger. Write a 0 and move on.

Keep going until you reach the far right heading, 1. The amount left should be 0 by then. It ends at 0 because every heading you took away adds up to your number. If it is not 0, check your take-aways.

blocks.watch: Always write all eight bits, even when the first bits are 0. A byte always has eight bits. For example, 19 is 16 + 2 + 1, so write 00010011, not 10011. In 2022, one answer left off its first 0s. It got only one mark out of two.

play.title: Your turn: denary to binary
play.lead: A random number appears. At each heading, answer one question: can the heading be taken from the amount left? Tap Yes or No and the bits fill in as you go.

exam.say: Show your working. Write each take-away where the answer is yes, like 147 − 128 = 19. The take-away steps earn a mark. Then write all eight bits.

try.stem: Which byte is the denary number 53?
try.why: Start with 53 left. 128 no, 64 no. 32 yes: 53 − 32 = 21 left. 16 yes: 21 − 16 = 5 left. 8 no. 4 yes: 5 − 4 = 1 left. 2 no. 1 yes: 0 left. So the bits are 0 0 1 1 0 1 0 1. That is 00110101.

screens.title: Hexadecimal: a short way to write binary
screens.goal: I can say why hex is used, and write any nibble as one hex digit.

anim.title: A short way to write a byte
anim.lead: Try copying this byte without a mistake: 11010110. It is easy to slip with eight 0s and 1s. Programmers write the same byte as D6. This short way is called [[hexadecimal|1]], or hex. Press Next to see how it works.
steps: The short way works one nibble at a time. A nibble has four bits, so it needs only four headings. Like a byte's, they start at 1 on the right and double: 8, 4, 2, 1. Start at 0000, which is 0. Count up: 0001 is 1, 0010 is 2, and so on. 1001 is 8 + 1 = 9. Up to 9, the hex digit is the same as the number.
Next comes 1010. That is 8 + 2 = ten. Ten needs two digits in denary. But hex writes each nibble as one digit, so ten is written A.
Keep counting. 1011 is 8 + 2 + 1 = eleven, B. 1100 is 8 + 4 = twelve, C. 1101 is 8 + 4 + 1 = thirteen, D. 1110 is 8 + 4 + 2 = fourteen, E. 1111 is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = fifteen, F.

1111 is the biggest a nibble can be. So F is the last hex digit. That makes sixteen hex digits: ten from 0 to 9, and six from A to F. To remember the letters, learn that A = 10. Then count on: B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15.
Now a whole byte: 10010011. Split it in the middle into two nibbles: 1001 and 0011. Each nibble uses the headings 8, 4, 2, 1.
1001 is 8 + 1 = 9, so its hex digit is 9. 0011 is 2 + 1 = 3, so its hex digit is 3.

Put the two digits side by side: 10010011 is 93 in hex. Read it as nine, three, not ninety-three, because each digit is one nibble. Hex 93 and denary 147 are the same byte, written two ways. Check: 10010011 is 128 + 16 + 2 + 1 = 147. Eight digits became two.
Back to the start: 11010110 splits into 1101 and 0110. 1101 is 8 + 4 + 1 = thirteen, D. 0110 is 4 + 2 = 6. So it is D6.

say: Hex writes each nibble as one digit. A byte is two nibbles, so every byte is just two hex digits.
A nibble has only four bits, so it needs only four headings. They start at 1 on the right and double: 8, 4, 2, 1. The smallest nibble, 0000, is 0. The biggest, 1111, is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15.
So a nibble can be any number from 0 to 15. Counting the 0, that is sixteen numbers. So hex needs sixteen single digits.
A number system's [[base|1]] is how many digits it uses. Denary uses ten digits, 0 to 9, so it is base 10. Binary uses two, 0 and 1, so it is base 2. Hex uses sixteen digits, so it is base 16.
Hex uses 0 to 9, then letters for 10 to 15:

picture.title: A short code for every nibble
lines: Look at the calendar page for SEPTEMBER. September is the ninth month of the year. So a date can write it as the number 9: 25 September becomes 25/9. The numbers in the grid are days, not months. Every month has its own number, and everyone uses the same ones.
Hex does the same for nibbles. Each of the sixteen different nibbles has its own one-digit code. 1011 is long to read, so it is written B. 0000 is 0, 1001 is 9, 1010 is A and 1111 is F.
In the Turn nibbles into hex box, the hex digit under each nibble is its code.
match: Every month has one number, the same for everyone
Every nibble has one hex digit, the same in every computer
picture.breaks: Months stop at 12, and 10, 11 and 12 take two digits. Hex has sixteen codes, and every one is a single digit. After 9, hex uses the six letters A, B, C, D, E and F. A hex digit is not just a label. Add the headings and you get its value.

img.alt: A calendar page headed SEPTEMBER. The days 1 to 30 sit in rows under Sun to Sat.
img.cap: A calendar page for September, the ninth month. In a date, September is written as 9.

note.title: Where you see hex: colour codes
lines: You will see hex in web colour codes like #FF6600. The # marks it as a colour code.
Then come three bytes in hex. FF says how much red light to mix. 66 says how much green, and 00 how much blue.
F is 1111, so FF is 11111111, the biggest a byte can be. So this colour has all the red it can have. 00 means no blue at all.

play.title: Turn nibbles into hex
play.lead: Set the right four switches to 1010. The bracket under them shows 8 + 2 = 10, which is hex A. Now make B, which is eleven: 8 + 2 + 1. Then make F, which is fifteen: all four on. Then set all eight switches to 11010110. Read the two hex digits one at a time: D, then 6.

exam.say: Hexadecimal is a base 16 number system. It uses the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F. Programmers use it to shorten long binary patterns: one hex digit stands for four bits. Uses: colour codes on web pages, and memory addresses. A memory address says where data is kept in memory. It works like a house number on a street. Memory addresses are often written in hex.

try.stem: Match each nibble to its hex digit.
try.why: 1010 is 8 + 2 = ten, which is A. 1111 is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = fifteen, which is F. 0011 is 2 + 1 = 3. 1100 is 8 + 4 = twelve, which is C.

screens.title: Hex and binary: one hex digit for each nibble
screens.goal: I can change a byte into two hex digits and back again.

anim.title: 11111011 to hex, then A9 back to binary
anim.lead: Press Next to change the byte 11111011 into hex. Then watch the hex code A9 go back into binary.
steps: Here is the byte 11111011. Press Next to cut it in the middle into two nibbles.
It is cut into two nibbles: 1111 and 1011. The left nibble is 1111. A nibble has four bits, so it uses the four headings 8, 4, 2, 1. So 1111 is 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15. Fifteen is F.
The right nibble is 1011. That is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. Eleven is B.
Write the two hex digits side by side. 11111011 is FB in hexadecimal.
Now the other way. The hex code A9 has two digits, A and 9. Each digit becomes one nibble of four bits.

A is 10. Play the take-away game with the headings 8, 4, 2, 1. Can 8 be taken from 10? Yes, so write 1. 10 − 8 = 2 left. Can 4 be taken from 2? No, so write 0. Can 2 be taken from 2? Yes, so write 1. 2 − 2 = 0 left. Can 1 be taken from 0? No, so write 0. So A is 1010.
Now 9. Can 8 be taken from 9? Yes, so write 1. 9 − 8 = 1 left. Can 4 be taken from 1? No, so write 0. Can 2 be taken from 1? No, so write 0. Can 1 be taken from 1? Yes, so write 1. So 9 is 1001.
Put the nibbles side by side. A9 is 10101001 in binary.

say: That was binary to hex. Cut the byte in the middle into two nibbles. That gives four bits on the left and four on the right.
Each nibble is only four bits, so it needs only four headings: 8, 4, 2, 1. Add the headings that have a 1 under them. Then write that value as one hex digit.
Values 0 to 9 stay as digits. Values 10 to 15 become letters:

Hex to binary goes the other way. Each hex digit becomes four bits. If the digit is a letter, change it into its number first, like A = 10. Then find the four bits with the take-away game, using the headings 8, 4, 2, 1.
The animation did this for A9. A became 1010 and 9 became 1001. Side by side, they make the byte 10101001.

play.title: Your turn: hex and binary
play.lead: The questions take turns: byte to hex, then hex to byte. Each step tells you what to tap. Press Another one for a new question.

exam.say: Split the byte into two nibbles. Convert each nibble to one hex digit. Hex to binary: convert each hex digit to 4 bits. Show the nibbles as working.

try.stem: What is the byte 10101100 in hexadecimal?
try.why: Split it: 1010 is 8 + 2 = ten, which is A. 1100 is 8 + 4 = twelve, which is C. So AC.

screens.title: Hex and denary: go through binary, then check with sixteens
screens.goal: I can change a hex code into denary and a denary number into hex, with working.

anim.title: Change the hex code E3 into denary, then check it
anim.lead: Press Next to change E3 into binary, then add the headings. Then check the answer a second way.
steps: Start with the hex code E3. E is one digit and 3 is the other.

E is 14. Play the take-away game with 8, 4, 2, 1. Can 8 be taken from 14? Yes, so write 1. 14 − 8 = 6 left. Can 4 be taken from 6? Yes, so write 1. 6 − 4 = 2 left. Can 2 be taken from 2? Yes, so write 1. 2 − 2 = 0 left. Can 1 be taken from 0? No, so write 0. So E is 1110.

Now 3. Can 8 or 4 be taken from 3? No, so write 0 under each. Can 2 be taken from 3? Yes, so write 1. 3 − 2 = 1 left. Can 1 be taken from 1? Yes, so write 1. 1 − 1 = 0 left. So 3 is 0011. Together, E3 is the byte 11100011.
Join the two nibbles into one byte. Write the eight headings, 128 to 1, over the whole byte. Add the headings that have a 1 under them: 128 + 64 + 32 + 2 + 1.

Now check with sixteens. Denary has ten digits, so the 2 in 27 counts tens. Hex has sixteen digits, so its left digit counts sixteens. E is 14, so that is 14 sixteens. Split 16 into 10 and 6 to make it easy. 14 × 10 = 140. 14 × 6 = 84, because 10 × 6 = 60 and 4 × 6 = 24. 140 + 84 = 224. Then 224 + 3 = 227. It matches.

say: That was the safe route for hex to denary. Change each hex digit into four bits. Join the two nibbles into one byte. Write 128 to 1 over the whole byte and add the headings with a 1. Do not add the two nibbles on their own: 14 + 3 = 17 is wrong. In the byte, the left nibble sits under 128, 64, 32 and 16. So it is worth far more than 14.

There is also a quick check. Hex has sixteen digits, and F is the last one. After F, which is fifteen, hex has run out of digits. So sixteen is written as hex 10, read one, zero. It means one sixteen and no ones.

Denary does the same after 9: ten is written 10, one ten and no ones. So in a two-digit hex code, the left digit counts sixteens. The right digit counts ones. In 27, the 2 counts tens. In E3, the E means 14 sixteens and the 3 means 3 ones.
The hex letters are:
So E3 is 14 sixteens plus 3. To work out 14 × 16, split 16 into 10 and 6, so each part is easy. 14 × 10 = 140. 14 × 6 = 84, because 10 × 6 = 60 and 4 × 6 = 24. 140 + 84 = 224. Then 224 + 3 = 227.

Denary to hex goes the other way. Change the number into eight bits with the take-away game. Then split the byte into nibbles. Take 227. Can 128 be taken from 227? Yes, so write 1. 227 − 128 = 99 left. Can 64 be taken from 99? Yes, so write 1. 99 − 64 = 35 left. Can 32 be taken from 35? Yes, so write 1. 35 − 32 = 3 left. Can 16, 8 or 4 be taken from 3? No, so write 0 under each. Can 2 be taken from 3? Yes, so write 1. 3 − 2 = 1 left. Can 1 be taken from 1? Yes, so write 1. 1 − 1 = 0 left. So 227 is 11100011.
Split 11100011 into 1110 and 0011. 1110 is 8 + 4 + 2 = 14, which is E. 0011 is 2 + 1 = 3. So 227 is E3 in hex.

blocks.watch: Hex letters can be capital or small: 9b and 9B are the same answer. In denary working, write numbers only: write 14 × 16, never E × 16. E is a hex digit, not a denary number.

play.title: Your turn: hex and denary
play.lead: The questions take turns: hex to denary, then denary to hex. Each step tells you what to do, and the working builds up as you go.

exam.say: For denary to hex, show the 8 bits split into two nibbles, then each hex digit. For hex to denary, show each hex digit as 4 bits and add the headings. Or show the sixteens check: E3 is 14 × 16 + 3. Either way, the working earns a mark.
exam.src: 2021 Q6(d), 2023 Q7(c)(i) and 2025 Q4(a)(ii) mark schemes

try.stem: What is the hex code FF in denary?
try.why: F is 15. The left F counts sixteens: 15 × 16. Split 16 into 10 and 6: 15 × 10 = 150. 15 × 6 = 90, because 10 × 6 = 60 and 5 × 6 = 30. 150 + 90 = 240. Add the 15 on the right: 240 + 15 = 255. FF is also 11111111, the biggest number a byte can hold.

screens.title: Adding two bytes and spotting overflow
screens.goal: I can add two bytes with carries and say what overflow does to the answer.

anim.title: Add two bytes, then see a sum that is too big
anim.lead: Adding binary works like adding denary. Go column by column from the right, and carry when a column gets too big. Press Next to add 01011011 and 00110111. Watch where the carries go. Then a second sum shows what happens when the answer is too big for a byte.
steps: Write the two bytes one above the other, headings on top. Start at the right-hand column, the one headed 1.
Column headed 1: 1 + 1 = 2. A column can only hold 0 or 1, so 2 is written 10 in binary. Write the 0. Carry the 1 into the next column to the left, as in denary.
Column headed 2: 1 + 1 + the carried 1 = 3. 3 is written 11 in binary. Write 1 and carry 1.
Column headed 4: 0 + 1 + the carried 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column headed 8: 1 + 0 + the carried 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column headed 16: 1 + 1 + the carried 1 = 3, which is 11 in binary. Write 1 and carry 1.
Column headed 32: 0 + 1 + the carried 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column headed 64: 1 + 0 + the carried 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary. Write 0 and carry 1.
Column headed 128: 0 + 0 + the carried 1 = 1. Write 1 with no carry. The answer is 10010010, which is 128 + 16 + 2 = 146.

Now a second sum: 11100011 + 01101110. 11100011 is 128 + 64 + 32 + 2 + 1 = 227. 01101110 is 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 110. 227 + 110 = 337. That is bigger than 255, the biggest a byte can hold. So the answer cannot fit in eight bits.

Add column by column, as before. The carries are in the carry row. The column headed 128 is 1 + 0 + the carried 1 = 2. Write 0 and carry 1. That carry has no column left. So the answer, 101010001, has nine bits. The 1 in the ninth column is overflow. In an exam, circle it like this.

The ninth bit is lost. The byte keeps only 01010001, which is 64 + 16 + 1 = 81. Headings double: 64, 128, 256. So the ninth bit was worth 256. 256 + 81 = 337, the true total. The adding was done right. But the byte has no room for the ninth bit. So the stored answer, 81, is wrong.

say: That was binary addition. It works like adding denary, column by column from the right. In each column, count the 1s, carry included. There are four facts to know.
0 + 0 = 0. 0 + 1 = 1. 1 + 1 = 2, which is written 10 in binary: write 0 and carry 1.
1 + 1 + 1 = 3, which is written 11 in binary: write 1 and carry 1.
Write the carry above the next column to the left. Then add that column, carry included.

A byte has room for only eight bits. If the last carry needs a ninth column, the ninth bit has nowhere to go. It is lost. That is called [[overflow|1]]. The adding was done right, but the stored answer is wrong.

picture.title: A car's mileage counter rolling over
lines: Look at the mileage counter in the photo. It has five wheels for whole miles. The white box on the right counts tenths, so ignore it. The most the five wheels can show is 99999.
Drive 1 more mile and every wheel rolls round to 0. The counter now says 00000.
The true total, 100000 miles, needs a sixth wheel for whole miles. There is none, so the 1 at the front is lost.
Drive 5 more miles from 99999 and the counter shows 00004. The true total is 100004. The front 1 is lost, but the rest is kept.
A byte has eight bits. When a sum needs a ninth bit, that bit is lost too. The other eight bits are kept. That is overflow.
match: The front 1 of 100000, which is lost
The ninth bit, which is lost
picture.breaks: Each wheel on the counter has ten digits, 0 to 9. Each column of a byte has only two, 0 and 1.

img.alt: A car's mileage counter shown three times: 99999.9, then the wheels turning, then all 0s.
img.cap: Top: 99999.9 miles. Middle: the wheels turning. Bottom: a tenth of a mile later, every wheel shows 0. The white box on the right counts tenths of a mile.

play.title: Add two bytes live
play.lead: Tap any bit in the two top rows to flip it. Watch the carry row and the Answer row. If the answer needs a ninth bit, it shows as the Overflow bit. The line under the sum then says what the byte keeps. Try to make the Overflow bit appear. Then make it go away.

exam.say: The answer is bigger than 255, the biggest number a byte can hold. The ninth bit, the overflow bit, is lost, so the stored answer is wrong.

parts.stem: Fill the gaps using the word bank.

surface.text: When 11111111 and 00000001 are added, the answer needs {1} bits. The extra bit is called {2}. It is {3}, so the stored answer is {4}.

parts.why: 11111111 + 00000001 = 100000000: nine bits. In denary that is 255 + 1 = 256. Headings double: 64, 128, 256. So the ninth bit is worth 256. A byte has no ninth heading, so that bit is overflow. It is lost, so the byte keeps 00000000, which is 0: incorrect.

parts.stem: Pick TRUE or FALSE for each statement about overflow.

rows: Overflow happens when the total needs more bits than the byte has.
The extra bit is kept in a ninth column of the byte.
The stored answer is smaller than the true total.
Overflow means the two bytes were added wrongly.

parts.why: The sum was done right, but a byte has only eight columns. The ninth bit is lost, so the stored answer is wrong and too small.

screens.title: Units of storage: bit to terabyte
screens.goal: I can order the storage units and pick the largest from a mixed list.

say: A byte is tiny. One phone photo is about 3,000,000 bytes. A number that long is hard to read and easy to get wrong. So bigger units are used, the way people say 3 kilometres, not 3,000 metres.

picture.title: A kilo of sugar
lines: Look at the bag of sugar in the photo. It says 1 kg. Kilo means a thousand, so the bag holds 1,000 grams.
Storage uses kilo too, with one twist. A kilobyte is 1,024 bytes, not 1,000. The reason for 1,024 comes below this picture.
match: One gram, the small unit the bag counts
One byte, the small unit a kilobyte counts
picture.breaks: Kilo on a bag of sugar means exactly 1,000. Kilo in kilobyte means 1,024, which is close to 1,000.

img.alt: A 1 kg bag of granulated sugar.
img.cap: 1 kg on the bag means 1,000 grams of sugar.

say: A [[kilobyte|1]] is 1,024 bytes. A [[megabyte|1]] is 1,024 kilobytes. 1,024 is close to 1,000. So a megabyte is about 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000 bytes, a million. So that phone photo of 3,000,000 bytes is about 3 megabytes.
A [[gigabyte|1]] is 1,024 megabytes. A [[terabyte|1]] is 1,024 gigabytes.

Why 1,024 and not 1,000? In denary, the headings are 1, 10, 100 and 1,000. These are the round numbers: each is ten times the last. In binary, the headings double each time instead. Computers count in binary, so the binary headings are their round numbers. Keep doubling past 128: 256, 512, 1,024. 1,024 is the binary heading nearest to 1,000. So 1,024 is the computer's kilo.
When you compare sizes, 1,000 is close enough to 1,024. So 2 terabytes is about 2,000 gigabytes. Use 1,024 when a question asks for the exact size.

To find the biggest amount, change every amount into the same unit first. Then compare the numbers. Which is bigger, 4,000 megabytes or 9,000 kilobytes? Change both into megabytes. 4,000 megabytes stays as 4,000 megabytes. 1,000 kilobytes is about 1 megabyte, so 9,000 kilobytes is about 9 megabytes. 4,000 is far bigger than 9. So 4,000 megabytes is bigger, even though 9,000 is the bigger number.
The same works one step up. 1,000 megabytes is about 1 gigabyte. So 5,000 megabytes is about 5 gigabytes.

screens.title: ASCII and Unicode: a number for every character
screens.goal: I can say what ASCII is, how many codes it has and why Unicode came.

say: Type a capital A on a keyboard. The computer stores the number 65, as the byte 01000001. Check: 64 + 1 = 65. Letters, digits and symbols are called characters. Every character is stored as a number like this.
The number comes from an agreed list. The first big agreed list was [[ASCII|1]]. It stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.

The original ASCII used 7 bits for each character. Seven bits make 128 patterns, from 0000000 up to 1111111. 1111111 is 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 127. Counting the 0, that is 128 codes. A 7-bit code is still stored in a full byte, with a 0 in front. So A, 1000001, is stored as 01000001.

Extended ASCII used 8 bits, a full byte. Eight bits make 256 patterns, from 00000000 up to 11111111. 11111111 is 255. Counting the 0, that is 256 codes. That is still far too few. Chinese alone has thousands of characters, and there are many other languages and emoji too.
Different countries filled the extra 128 codes differently. One code showed é in one country and a different letter in another. So a file could show the wrong letters in another country.
[[Unicode|1]] fixes this with a code for every character in every language, emoji included. No two characters share a code. So a file shows the same letters in every country.

The first 128 Unicode codes are the ASCII codes, so old text still works. A is 65 in both. Seven bits fit in one byte, so an ASCII character takes 1 byte. One byte has only 256 patterns. Unicode has far more codes than that, so some need two, three or four bytes.

picture.title: A phone book
lines: A phone book is a printed list of names, each with its phone number. A character code does the same for characters: each character gets a number.
ASCII is like a small phone book. It only has room for 128 names, or 256 in extended ASCII.

Unicode is like a phone book for the whole world. Every character in every language has its own number, emoji too. Pretend the world book copied the first 128 entries of the small book. Each one kept its number. That is what Unicode did with ASCII: A is 65 in both.
match: Unicode, every character in every language
The code number for a character
The small book's 128 entries, copied into the world book
Unicode's first 128 codes are the ASCII codes
picture.breaks: A new phone book comes out every year, and people's numbers can change. A Unicode code never changes: A is 65 for good. New codes are only added, such as new emoji.

exam.say: ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange. 7-bit ASCII represents 128 characters and 8-bit ASCII represents 256 characters. Unicode was introduced because ASCII could not represent the characters of every language. The extended codes also clashed between regions. Unicode represents every character in every language, including emoji. ASCII is the first part of Unicode. Some Unicode characters need more bits, so more storage.

screens.title: Data types: which kind of value is it?
screens.goal: I can name the data types and choose the right one for a variable.

say: A football app keeps the number of goals scored, say 3. It keeps it in a [[variable|1]] called goalsScored. A variable is a named box whose value can change. After another goal, goalsScored holds 4. Every variable has a [[data type|1]]. The type tells the computer what kind of value the variable holds. goalsScored only ever holds whole numbers. So its type is integer, the type for whole numbers.
An [[integer|1]] is a whole number, positive or negative, with no decimal part. A count of goals is an integer.
A [[real|1]] number can have a decimal part. A price like 1.99 is real. Some programming languages call a real a double or a float.
A [[character|1]] is one single letter, digit or symbol, like the grade B. The character '7' is only a symbol: you cannot do sums with it.

A [[string|1]] is a run of characters, like a name or the postcode BT34 2EX. A postcode has letters in it, so it is text. Text is stored as a string. Some text is all digits, like the phone number 07700 900123. You never do sums with a phone number. As a number, 07700 900123 would lose its first 0, the way 07 is just 7. So a phone number is a string too.
A [[Boolean|1]] holds only true or false. Has the pupil passed? True or false.
A [[date/time|1]] type holds a date, a time, or both. The computer can then add days or compare two times.
A name like passFail or isValid is a clue. Each name asks a yes or no question. So each holds true or false, and is a Boolean.

picture.title: Jars on a shelf
lines: Look at the jars in the photo. Two have labels: one says coconut flour and one says chia seed. Each label tells you what is in its jar.

Now picture a shelf of jars for data, each with a label. One label says whole numbers only. One says numbers with a decimal point. One says one character only: a single letter, digit or symbol. One says text: any run of characters.
Two more jars: one holds only true or false, and one holds only dates and times. A price like 1.99 does not fit the whole numbers jar: the program shows an error.

screens.title: Boolean logic: AND, OR and NOT truth tables
screens.goal: I can work out AND, OR and NOT and fill every cell of a truth table.

picture.title: Two buttons, a doorbell and a fridge light
lines: Look at the machine control in the photo. It has a green button at each end. Ignore the red and yellow buttons in the middle. The machine only runs while both buttons are pressed. Both hands must stay on the buttons. So neither hand can be under the machine while it runs. That is AND.
Picture a house with a bell button at the front door and the back door. The bell rings when either button is pressed, or both. That is OR.

Inside a fridge is a small switch that the door presses when it shuts. Switch pressed = 1, light off = 0. Switch not pressed = 0, light on = 1. The light is always the opposite of the switch. That is NOT.
In Play with it below, switches A and B are like the two buttons. The lamp is like the machine.
match: Both buttons pressed before the machine runs
Either doorbell button rings the bell
The fridge light doing the opposite of its door switch
picture.breaks: Real buttons can stick or break. A Boolean value is always exactly 0 or 1.

img.alt: An orange control box on a stand, with a green button at each end.
img.cap: A two-hand control. The machine only runs while both green buttons are pressed.
img.credit: Photo: Sam D. Wilbur, CC BY 4.0

say: The two buttons, the doorbell and the fridge light each follow a rule. Computers make decisions with the same three rules: AND, OR and NOT. 1 means true and 0 means false.

A [[truth table|1]] lists every possible input and the output the rule gives. An input is a value going into the rule. The output is what comes out. Each input has two choices, 0 or 1. So two inputs give 2 × 2 = 4 rows. Row 1 is A = 0, B = 0. Row 2 is A = 0, B = 1. Row 3 is A = 1, B = 0. Row 4 is A = 1, B = 1.
[[AND|1]] gives 1 only when both inputs are 1. [[OR|1]] gives 1 when either input is 1, or both.
[[NOT|1]] has one input and flips it. NOT 1 is 0 and NOT 0 is 1. With one input, its truth table has only 2 rows.

play.title: Two switches, one lamp
play.lead: Pick a rule, then flip switch A and switch B. Watch the lamp and the truth table row light up. NOT has only one input, so it uses switch A only. The lamp shows the output.

say: Some questions join two rules together, like NOT(P AND Q). P and Q are names for two inputs, like switches A and B.
The brackets are worked out first. So first work out P AND Q. Then apply NOT to that answer. The animation below does this for every row.
Rules can also be chained, one after another. Say X is 1. Y is 1 too. Z is X AND Y, so Z is 1 AND 1, which is 1. W is NOT Z, so W is NOT 1, which is 0.

anim.title: Fill in NOT(P AND Q), row by row
anim.lead: Press Next to fill one row at a time. The brackets are worked out first, then NOT flips the answer.
steps: An exam paper gives P, Q and two empty columns. The P AND Q column is your working. The NOT(P AND Q) column is the answer. Four rows cover every input.
Row 1: P is 0 and Q is 0. Neither is 1, so P AND Q is 0: write 0 in the working column. NOT 0 is 1, so write 1 in the answer column.
Row 2: P is 0 and Q is 1. Only Q is 1, so P AND Q is 0: write 0 in the working column. NOT 0 is 1, so write 1 in the answer column.
Row 3: P is 1 and Q is 0. Only P is 1, so P AND Q is 0: write 0 in the working column. NOT 0 is 1, so write 1 in the answer column.
Row 4: P is 1 and Q is 1. Both are 1, so P AND Q is 1: write 1 in the working column. NOT 1 is 0, so write 0 in the answer column.
Every cell is filled. The answer column, NOT(P AND Q), reads 1, 1, 1, 0. Each cell or column can earn its own mark.

exam.say: AND: the output is 1 only when all inputs are 1. OR: the output is 1 when any input is 1. NOT: the output is the opposite of the input. Work out any brackets first. Fill every empty cell. Each cell or column can earn its own mark.
exam.src: 2019 Q8(e), 2023 Q1(c) and 2024 Q4(e) mark schemes

try.stem: A = 1. B = 0. C is NOT B. D is A AND C. E is C OR D. Pick TRUE or FALSE for each line.
try.why: NOT 0 is 1, so C is 1. A AND C is 1 AND 1, so D is 1. C OR D is 1 OR 1, which is 1. So E is 1, not 0.
